When an interactive agent session drops in the middle of validation, it usually leaves behind a broken pipe and an ambiguous outcome.

As a builder, I have watched suites fail simply because the terminal connection closed before the workload finished running. This failure path confuses network interruptions with actual product regressions, destroying the confidence we need before we ship. Long-running validation cannot remain tied to the lifespan of an ephemeral client.

To solve this, we decoupled caller connectivity from suite execution. When an operator triggers vrooli scenario test, the command registers the request and returns immediately. It does not force the caller to hold an open session while the scenario executes. Instead, our background test engine, test-genie, takes ownership of the scenario test run the moment registration completes.

This handoff fundamentally changes how validation behaves. Because test-genie holds the run, execution continues uninterrupted even if the caller disconnects. The logs, identity, and intermediate state stay anchored to the server rather than vanishing with an abandoned local process. A builder or automated agent can step away without wondering whether a network glitch terminated the job.

We shipped this decoupling so that test execution survives transient client loss. Once a run is registered, it becomes a server-owned process with its own durable lifecycle. That means the caller can reconnect or wait on the result later, while the actual validation moves forward on stable ground, collecting reliable evidence for the next review.

The protocol documented in docs/TESTING.md establishes how this server-owned architecture replaces fragile client polling with a predictable, durable wait mechanism.

In conventional workflows, an orchestrating agent or builder usually has to maintain an active polling loop. That client repeatedly queries an endpoint, parses partial output, and risks network drops at every retry interval. Each dropped poll introduces an artificial failure path, cluttering telemetry with retry noise and making it difficult to know whether the test failed or the polling script died.

We replaced that fragility with a clean, single-point interface. When an operator starts a suite, they record its run identifier and execute test-genie runs wait --json. Instead of running a noisy status loop, this command blocks once on the server-owned run until execution reaches a terminal state. Custody of the execution remains strictly with test-genie, keeping state transitions contained on the server.

This approach transforms operational handoffs. When long-running validation spans multiple agent shifts or team members, the incoming operator does not need to inherit local state, terminal buffers, or fragile client-side timers. They only need the recorded run identifier to wait once on the existing run and capture the structured output directly.

We shipped this workflow because reliable validation requires absolute clarity about where work happens and where evidence lives. Moving from active client polling to a server-owned wait protocol prevents dropped network packets from corrupting our validation records. The test runs to completion under test-genie, and the final evidence remains addressable, structured, and ready for inspection the instant the wait unblocks.

A disconnected terminal should never be mistaken for a broken build. In distributed systems and long validation loops, confusing a dropped connection with a test failure creates a costly failure path: engineers spend hours chasing phantom regressions that were actually network hiccups.

We explicitly disentangled client lifecycle events from suite lifecycle states so that our validation records remain honest. In our execution model, a cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. When a terminal session terminates, an interactive agent disconnects, or a local network pipe breaks, test-genie does not panic or tear down the environment. The server-owned run simply continues along its path, accumulating logs and executing validation steps independently.

When an operator actually needs to stop a running scenario—perhaps because a bad commit was pushed or resources must be reallocated—they do not rely on closing their shell. Instead, they explicitly issue vrooli scenario test abort to tell test-genie to stop the suite. This command ends the run itself on the control plane, marking the run record appropriately and distinguishing an intentional abort from an accidental client disconnection.

This clear boundary preserves actionable evidence. When a builder examines the results, they can immediately distinguish between an infrastructure interruption on the client side and an authentic scenario failure on the server. If a client disconnected prematurely, an operator can still wait on or inspect the ongoing execution without invalidating the run.

We shipped this distinction because reliable telemetry requires precision around why execution stopped. By enforcing that only an explicit vrooli scenario test abort can terminate a suite, we protect the integrity of every scenario test run and ensure our team acts on genuine product defects rather than ambient client instability.

By transforming validation into an autonomous control plane, we changed the operational relationship between human builders, automated agents, and running workloads.

When long-running validation operates as a server-owned process, test suites no longer behave like fragile terminal scripts. Instead, our background engine, test-genie, coordinates scenario execution as a governed, persistent capability. A builder can register a suite, pass the identifier to a teammate or agent, and let that collaborator execute test-genie runs wait --json whenever they need to capture the final results.

This architecture makes collaborative engineering workflows genuinely durable. Because execution state lives on the server rather than within a fleeting terminal process, multiple workers can inspect the same immutable run without disrupting ongoing steps. Whether an autonomous agent checks progress or an on-call engineer steps in later to evaluate logs, the execution evidence remains addressable, verifiable, and complete. The failure path was predictable: a developer closed a laptop, an agent detached from a terminal, and the entire validation run evaporated into unrecorded noise. Treating every client drop as a broken build stripped away the evidence we needed to evaluate product stability.

We redesigned our testing lifecycle to ensure long execution does not depend on an open shell. In our testing protocol documented in docs/TESTING.md, we established that validation suites must exist as server-owned resources rather than ephemeral local processes. When an agent disconnects, the run itself should survive intact.

To achieve this, we decoupled test initiation from test observation. An operator begins execution with vrooli scenario test, which starts a scenario suite and returns once the run is registered. Instead of holding an active socket open for hours, the command hands off lifecycle management immediately to test-genie, our execution service that owns a scenario test run after the command returns.

This architecture ensures that the suite keeps its identity, logs, and verifiable evidence regardless of what happens to the caller. Disconnecting a terminal no longer halts execution, turning the simple act to wait into a durable, governed capability for every builder on the team.

Once registration completes, the client yields a discrete run identifier. As a builder, having an explicit identifier anchored in the server control plane changes the interaction model completely. The calling process no longer needs to babysit execution or maintain a fragile socket. Instead, test-genie manages the lifecycle autonomously in the background, treating the suite as a first-class operational entity.

The traditional failure path in detached architectures is relying on noisy client-side polling loops that repeatedly query status endpoints. Polling introduces race conditions, wastes network bandwidth, and clutters server logs with redundant read requests. We replaced that fragile pattern with a direct, single-call synchronization mechanism.

To observe the outcome without maintaining an active polling script, an operator invokes test-genie runs wait --json, which blocks once on a server-owned run and serves as the documented alternative to polling. This approach creates a deterministic boundary: the command sleeps cleanly at the transport level until the execution environment emits a final status payload.

This shift matters because it decouples validation progress from connection stability. A builder can launch a suite in an automated continuous integration step, hand the run identifier to another system, or simply reconnect later to wait for the final artifact. Because test-genie preserves the full context on the server, any authorized agent can query the registered run without risking test interruption.

By separating run initialization from result collection, we turned validation into a reliable background asset. The suite executes according to its own schedule, and the caller only rejoins when it is ready to consume the completed evidence.

Maintaining this detached model requires a strict operational boundary between dropped transport sessions and intentional test cancellation. When an operator's terminal closes or an automated pipeline times out, the client connection is cancelled, but the suite itself must keep executing. A cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. Conflating the two creates an ambiguous failure path where a builder cannot tell whether a red status reflects a network drop or a true product defect.

In a system where disconnected callers kill background work, every transport glitch masquerades as a software bug. That ambiguity erodes confidence in automated verification because developers waste time debugging missing records rather than actual test failures. To preserve uncorrupted validation evidence, the control plane must treat the loss of a listening client as an irrelevant transport event rather than an instruction to tear down the environment.

When an operator genuinely needs to halt validation, that intention must be explicit. To terminate execution intentionally, the builder issues vrooli scenario test abort, which ends the run itself, as opposed to cancelling the client. This command communicates directly with test-genie to stop the server-owned process, finalize the record, and mark the suite as terminated by human request.

Drawing this clear line protects the integrity of our diagnostics. If a client drops, the server-owned run continues undisturbed, allowing another operator to attach and wait for the true result. If a run is explicitly stopped using vrooli scenario test abort, the evidence reflects a deliberate operational choice. Separating connection state from run lifecycle ensures every reported failure maps to authentic test outcomes rather than fragile client sessions.

This operational decoupling transforms validation from a transient local task into an asynchronous foundation for entire engineering teams. When execution is server-owned, handoffs between builders stop depending on shared terminal histories, fragile screen sessions, or ambient chat context. One engineer can register a validation suite before stepping away, and an entirely different builder can later connect to the control plane, inspect the ongoing progress, and execute test-genie runs wait --json to receive the verified outcome directly.

By delegating ownership to test-genie, we established a reliable contract across our release pipeline. Autonomous systems, automated continuous integration triggers, and human operators all interface with the exact same durable test identity. No single participant has to remain glued to a live socket simply to shepherd long-running suites to completion. Instead, the testing infrastructure guarantees that all execution logs, intermediate states, and final assertions remain addressable on the server until someone needs to evaluate them.

This continuity fundamentally changes how we make release decisions. When failure paths are isolated to real product defects rather than severed connections, the data recorded in the system becomes genuinely trustworthy. We no longer ask whether an incomplete test run was an operational accident or a true code regression; the durable record answers that question definitively.

Ultimately, shifting to server-owned validation turns what used to be dead waiting time into a governed, collaborative capability. By allowing any agent or developer to step in and wait on a persistent test lifecycle, we built a workflow where validation keeps moving forward even when our workstations close.

When an interactive terminal drops midway through a long validation suite, traditional tooling creates a deceptive failure path. It conflates a severed connection with a genuine product defect, corrupting validation evidence. I shipped this update because builders need dependable signals rather than phantom test regressions caused by ephemeral shell disconnections.

We established the foundation for decoupled execution in `docs/TESTING.md`. The core principle is straightforward: the execution boundary must survive beyond the lifespan of the client process that initiated it. When an agent or operator starts a validation suite using `vrooli scenario test`, the command registers the workload and returns immediately.

From that exact moment, our background coordinator `test-genie` takes full ownership of the execution lifecycle. This makes the execution run completely server-owned instead of tethered to the local machine. The suite continues executing independently of network hiccups or closed laptops.

Because `test-genie` retains custody of the run, the entire validation state remains intact. We no longer ask an operator to maintain an open shell just to keep a test alive. Instead, the caller can safely disconnect or wait on demand, knowing the underlying evidence is protected from client-level disruptions.

As a builder, separating the client lifecycle from the server lifecycle introduces an essential operational distinction: a cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. If an agent process exits abruptly or an interactive terminal connection drops, the server-owned execution proceeds untouched. We deliberately separated these two events so that lost network connectivity never forces a false failure path onto a healthy validation suite.

When an operator actually intends to terminate an active validation workload, they must declare that intent explicitly rather than relying on client disconnects as a side effect. Running `vrooli scenario test abort` ends the run itself, as opposed to cancelling the client. This dedicated command communicates directly with the coordinator, ensuring that execution ceases only when an operator or automation workflow purposefully decides to stop the validation process.

Treating client cancellation and test abortion as separate operations preserves valuable validation evidence. In distributed environments, local shell interruptions should never invalidate hours of background execution or destroy diagnostic artifacts before they can be reviewed. By making this distinction concrete, we shipped a workflow where an aborted run represents an explicit, intentional choice, while a disconnected client remains a harmless event that leaves the validation record intact.

Once a suite is registered, tracking its completion without wasting network cycles or introducing noisy loops becomes the next operational challenge. Instead of writing custom retry scripts or hammering an endpoint, we shipped a direct synchronization mechanism. Running test-genie runs wait --json blocks once on a server-owned run as the documented alternative to polling.

This command transforms how an agent or human operator interacts with long-running validation. The workflow requires only that the operator records the run identifier generated at registration time. With that handle saved, any subsequent process can reattach to the server-owned workload at any point. You invoke the command, allow it to wait efficiently on the coordinator, and receive the structured outcome the moment execution concludes.

Eliminating client-driven polling loops removes unnecessary protocol noise and prevents the flaky timeouts that often corrupt automated pipelines. When a long-running suite takes hours, an agent does not need to stay actively tethered or repeatedly ask whether results are ready. The waiting mechanism turns synchronization into a clean, single-point event managed entirely by test-genie.

By blocking cleanly on the background coordinator, the system preserves the integrity of validation records across disjointed session boundaries. An operator can initiate a run in one session, hand the run identifier to a downstream automation agent in another environment, and let that process wait for the definitive result. This ensures durable synchronization without fragile client loops.

By decoupling execution lifecycles from interactive caller sessions, we turned long-running validation into an operational control plane capability. In complex environments, the primary failure path is often not software bugs, but the fragility of the validation harness itself. When an infrastructure interruption occurs, a server-owned execution ensures that test-genie preserves every log, status, and diagnostic trace rather than dropping them into the void.

This persistence fundamentally changes how teams organize automated work. Instead of forcing an engineer or automation agent to maintain continuous custody over a single shell, validation becomes an addressable, asynchronous artifact. One builder can trigger a suite, disconnect without penalty, and let another teammate or downstream process wait on the exact same server-owned record. The execution retains its identity across tool boundaries, eliminating the ambiguity between a network hiccup and a genuine product defect.

Making validation durable converts passive waiting into a governed platform primitive. Because test-genie manages the entire run independently, the system can reliably self-validate and coordinate complex validation lifecycles without human babysitting. We shipped this architecture in docs/TESTING.md to give builders absolute confidence in their signals, turning validation handoffs into a deterministic, dependable operational process.
